lessonTitle: Connective Tissue Disease and Vasculitis: SLE, Autoantibodies and Giant Cell Arteritis

blocks.text: A 27-year-old woman returns from a beach holiday with a red rash across her cheeks, painful swollen finger joints, mouth ulcers and urine that looks frothy. Her GP's blood test shows a positive antinuclear antibody and she has been frightened by an internet search. Whether that single result matters depends entirely on the person it was ordered for, and that is the heart of this unit.

blocks.markdown: **Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)** is a chronic autoimmune disease in which loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens produces autoantibodies and immune complexes that deposit in tissues and activate complement, causing inflammation in many organs. It most often affects women of child-bearing age, and is more frequent and often more severe in people of African, Caribbean and Asian ancestry. Ultraviolet light is a classic trigger because it increases apoptotic cell debris that exposes nuclear antigens. The course is relapsing and remitting.

rows: Malar (butterfly) rash sparing the nasolabial folds; photosensitivity; discoid lesions; alopecia
Non-erosive inflammatory arthritis or arthralgia of small joints
Lupus nephritis: haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, raised creatinine
Seizures, psychosis, cognitive and mood disturbance, stroke
Haemolytic anaemia, leucopenia or lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia
Antiphospholipid syndrome with thrombosis and recurrent miscarriage; accelerated atherosclerosis
blocks.caption: Multisystem features of SLE.

blocks.title: Why renal checks matter
blocks.text: Lupus nephritis is often silent early. Urinalysis for protein and blood and a urine protein-to-creatinine or albumin-to-creatinine ratio, blood pressure and renal function are checked in everyone with suspected or established SLE. Early nephritis is treated with immunosuppression after specialist assessment and often renal biopsy.

blocks.markdown: **Autoantibody tests and their limits.** An autoantibody test is only as useful as the probability of disease before it was ordered. **Antinuclear antibody (ANA)**, usually detected by immunofluorescence on cells, is present in over 95 percent of people with SLE, so a negative ANA makes SLE very unlikely (high sensitivity), but it is also positive in a substantial minority of healthy people (more at low titres and in older adults) and in other autoimmune diseases, infections and with some drugs, so it has poor specificity. Therefore ANA is requested only when there is a reasonable clinical suspicion of a connective tissue disease. Specific antibodies then help classify and monitor disease.

rows: SLE, Sjogren syndrome, systemic sclerosis, mixed connective tissue disease; also healthy people
Sensitive, not specific; titre and pattern help; a screening test
Highly specific; levels often track disease activity and lupus nephritis
Very specific but only present in a minority
Cross the placenta: risk of neonatal lupus and congenital heart block
Supports small-vessel vasculitis; specific antigen tests (PR3 or MPO) are needed
blocks.caption: Autoantibodies, associations and interpretation (patterns vary by laboratory).
PPV = positive predictive value: the probability of disease given a positive test. Prevalence here means the pre-test probability in the group tested.

blocks.title: A positive ANA in a low-risk population
blocks.prompt: In a clinic of 1000 patients with non-specific aches, the prevalence of SLE is 5 percent. ANA has sensitivity 95 percent and specificity 80 percent. What is the positive predictive value?

steps.text: People with SLE: 1000 x 0.05 = 50. People without: 950.
True positives = 50 x 0.95 = 47.5; false positives = 950 x (1 - 0.80) = 190.

Only about 1 in 5 positive results reflects SLE, because most positives come from the large non-lupus group. The test should therefore be ordered when features such as photosensitive rash, serositis or cytopenias raise the pre-test probability, and a positive result should be followed by specific antibodies and clinical assessment.

blocks.answer: PPV is 20 percent: a positive ANA in a low-prevalence group is more often a false than a true positive.

blocks.markdown: **Vasculitis** is inflammation of blood vessel walls, classified by vessel size. **Large-vessel**: giant cell arteritis (GCA) and Takayasu arteritis. **Medium-vessel**: polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease. **Small-vessel**: ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis) and IgA vasculitis. Features include fever, weight loss, palpable purpura, mononeuritis multiplex, glomerulonephritis, and pulmonary haemorrhage in small-vessel disease.

**Giant cell arteritis (GCA)** is a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium arteries, almost exclusively in people over 50, often with polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). It presents with a new headache, scalp tenderness, **jaw claudication** (pain on chewing), systemic upset and **visual symptoms** such as transient visual loss (amaurosis fugax) or double vision. Inflammation of the ophthalmic and posterior ciliary arteries can cause **sudden irreversible blindness** from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, sometimes in the second eye within days if untreated. ESR and CRP are usually markedly raised, platelets may be raised, and the temporal artery may be tender or have reduced pulsation.

blocks.title: Acting on suspected GCA
blocks.prompt: A 74-year-old woman has 3 weeks of new left-sided temporal headache, jaw pain on chewing and scalp tenderness when brushing her hair. ESR is 92 mm/h and CRP 80 mg/L. Visual acuity is normal. What do you do?

steps.text: Features (age over 50, new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, high inflammatory markers) make GCA likely.
The urgent concern is sight: vision loss is irreversible and can occur suddenly, so treatment starts on clinical suspicion, without waiting for a biopsy or ultrasound.

Start high-dose glucocorticoid immediately (commonly prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily if there are no visual symptoms; with visual loss, higher-dose intravenous treatment per local and British Society for Rheumatology guidance; check the BNF and local pathway).

Arrange urgent specialist assessment through the local fast-track pathway, with temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy (biopsy remains useful for some days after starting steroids). Add gastroprotection and bone protection, and counsel about visual symptoms: report any change immediately.

blocks.answer: Start high-dose steroids immediately and arrange urgent confirmation; do not wait for biopsy.

items: Suspect GCA in anyone over 50 with new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual symptoms or PMR with systemic symptoms.
Send ESR, CRP and full blood count, but do not delay steroids for results if clinical suspicion is high.
Start glucocorticoid at once; any visual symptoms mean emergency same-day specialist or ophthalmology assessment.
Confirm with temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign) or biopsy; steroids are tapered slowly over many months with steroid-sparing agents considered by specialists.
Monitor for steroid adverse effects: bone protection, glucose, blood pressure, infection.

blocks.title: Urgency
blocks.text: In GCA, delay in starting steroids can mean permanent loss of vision. Waiting for a biopsy before treating is a recognised and avoidable cause of blindness.

points: SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease (skin, joints, serosa, kidney, nervous system, blood) affecting young women, with nephritis often silent and needing regular urine and blood pressure checks.

ANA is sensitive but not specific, so it should be requested only when pre-test probability is meaningful; anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are specific, low complement indicates activity, and anti-Ro carries neonatal lupus risk.
Giant cell arteritis (over 50, new headache, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, raised ESR/CRP) requires high-dose steroids immediately to prevent blindness, followed by confirmation.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has a photosensitive facial rash sparing the nasolabial folds, painless oral ulcers, symmetrical non-erosive finger arthritis and pleuritic chest pain. Which diagnosis best unifies these features?

distractorRationale.a: RA does not cause a malar rash, oral ulcers or serositis, and is erosive.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: malar rash, oral ulcers, non-erosive arthritis and serositis form a classic SLE picture.
distractorRationale.c: GCA affects people over 50 with headache and visual symptoms.

questions.explanation: SLE is a multisystem disease. Photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, oral ulcers, non-erosive arthritis and serositis together point strongly to SLE.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with known SLE develops frothy urine and new hypertension. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein and blood. Her anti-dsDNA titre has risen and C3 and C4 are low. What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Probable lupus nephritis; check urine protein-to-creatinine ratio and renal function and arrange urgent specialist assessment including renal biopsy
Urinary tract infection; give antibiotics only

questions.correctOptionText: Probable lupus nephritis; check urine protein-to-creatinine ratio and renal function and arrange urgent specialist assessment including renal biopsy

distractorRationale.a: Infection could coexist but does not explain hypertension, low complement and a rising anti-dsDNA.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: rising anti-dsDNA with low complement and proteinuric haematuria indicates active lupus nephritis.
distractorRationale.c: Proteinuria with hypertension is not normal.
distractorRationale.d: NSAIDs can worsen renal function, and RA is not the diagnosis.

questions.explanation: Rising anti-dsDNA, low complement and proteinuria with haematuria in a patient with SLE indicate active lupus nephritis. Management requires prompt assessment, often renal biopsy, and immunosuppression; NSAIDs should be avoided.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with 6 months of fatigue and no other findings has a positive antinuclear antibody at a titre of 1 in 80. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The result is non-specific: ANA is positive in a notable proportion of healthy people, so interpretation depends on clinical features and the pre-test probability
ANA is specific for SLE and no further tests are required
A positive ANA excludes rheumatoid arthritis

questions.correctOptionText: The result is non-specific: ANA is positive in a notable proportion of healthy people, so interpretation depends on clinical features and the pre-test probability

distractorRationale.a: ANA has poor specificity and cannot establish SLE by itself.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: ANA is sensitive but not specific, so a low-titre result in the absence of suggestive features is often not significant.
distractorRationale.c: Specific tests and clinical assessment are needed.
distractorRationale.d: ANA says nothing about excluding RA.

questions.explanation: ANA is a sensitive screening test with low specificity. A low-titre positive result in a patient with only fatigue most likely does not indicate SLE; the interpretation depends on clinical features and, if suggestive, specific antibodies such as anti-dsDNA.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with Sjogren syndrome is 12 weeks pregnant. Which antibody is most relevant to the risk of neonatal lupus and congenital heart block?

distractorRationale.a: Anti-dsDNA relates to SLE activity and nephritis, not neonatal heart block.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: anti-Ro (and anti-La) antibodies cross the placenta and can cause neonatal lupus and congenital heart block.
distractorRationale.c: Anti-centromere is associated with limited systemic sclerosis.
distractorRationale.d: RF does not cause neonatal lupus.

questions.explanation: Anti-Ro and anti-La IgG antibodies cross the placenta and can injure the fetal conduction system and skin. Mothers with these antibodies need specialist obstetric and fetal heart monitoring.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has had 2 days of scalp tenderness while combing her hair and today had 5 minutes of complete loss of vision in her right eye that recovered. ESR is 70 mm/h. The specialist clinic cannot see her until next week. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Wait for the clinic and temporal artery biopsy before treating
Start high-dose glucocorticoid now and arrange urgent same-day specialist or ophthalmology assessment
Prescribe paracetamol and review in a week

questions.correctOptionText: Start high-dose glucocorticoid now and arrange urgent same-day specialist or ophthalmology assessment

distractorRationale.b: Correct: transient visual loss suggests imminent ischaemic optic neuropathy; steroids start at once with urgent assessment.
distractorRationale.c: This is not safe: delay can cause irreversible sight loss.
distractorRationale.d: Antibiotics have no role in GCA.

questions.explanation: Transient visual loss with scalp tenderness and a high ESR strongly suggests giant cell arteritis with imminent risk of permanent blindness. High-dose glucocorticoid is started immediately on suspicion, with urgent assessment for confirmation (dose and route per BNF/local and BSR guidance).

questions.stem: In suspected giant cell arteritis, steroid treatment should be withheld until temporal artery biopsy has confirmed the diagnosis.
questions.explanation: Treatment starts on clinical suspicion because vision loss is irreversible. Biopsy remains informative for a period after starting steroids, so confirmation is arranged urgently without delaying therapy.

questions.stem: In a clinic of 1000 patients the prevalence of SLE is 2 percent. An ANA test has sensitivity 95 percent and specificity 85 percent. What is the positive predictive value of a positive ANA, in percent?
questions.explanation: True positives = 20 x 0.95 = 19. False positives = 980 x 0.15 = 147. PPV = 19/(19+147) = 19/166 = 11.4 percent. A positive ANA in a low-prevalence group is far more often false than true.

questions.stem: Describe the multisystem features of systemic lupus erythematosus and explain why urine testing is routine in patients with SLE.
markingGuide: Skin: malar rash sparing nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, discoid lesions, alopecia; oral ulcers
Joints: non-erosive arthritis; serosa: pleuritis, pericarditis
Kidney: lupus nephritis (haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension); neuropsychiatric features such as seizures and psychosis
Haematological: haemolytic anaemia, leucopenia/lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia; antiphospholipid syndrome
Nephritis can be silent and damages kidneys early, so urinalysis, protein-to-creatinine ratio, blood pressure and renal function are monitored; early treatment preserves renal function
questions.explanation: SLE results from immune complex and autoantibody-mediated inflammation across organs. Silent but treatable renal disease justifies routine urinalysis.

questions.stem: Explain the roles and limitations of ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, complement, anti-Ro and ANCA in the investigation of suspected connective tissue disease or vasculitis.
markingGuide: ANA: sensitive (over 95 percent in SLE) but not specific; positive in healthy people, other autoimmune diseases, infections, drugs; screening test
Anti-dsDNA: specific for SLE, levels track disease activity and nephritis
Anti-Sm: highly specific but in a minority
Low C3 and C4 indicate active disease through complement consumption
Anti-Ro/La: associated with Sjogren and SLE; neonatal lupus and congenital heart block
ANCA (PR3, MPO): supports small-vessel vasculitis but needs clinical correlation
Pre-test probability and clinical context determine usefulness; avoid indiscriminate testing
questions.explanation: Autoantibody tests support but never replace clinical judgement. Their predictive value depends on the prevalence of disease in the group tested.

questions.stem: Outline the clinical features of giant cell arteritis and explain why treatment must not wait for confirmatory tests.
markingGuide: Age over 50; new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, systemic upset, polymyalgia rheumatica, raised ESR and CRP
Visual symptoms: transient visual loss, diplopia, sudden blindness from ischaemic optic neuropathy
Risk of irreversible blindness, potentially in the second eye, if untreated
Start high-dose glucocorticoid immediately on clinical suspicion (dose per BNF/BSR/local guidance)
Confirm with temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy; biopsy yield persists for some days after starting steroids
Bone protection and gastroprotection; slow taper with specialist follow-up
questions.explanation: The risk of permanent visual loss outweighs the small harm of brief steroid exposure before confirmation, so treatment begins on clinical suspicion.
